newsitem.title: USA: Dollar rises on strong U.S. data.
newsitem.headline: Dollar rises on strong U.S. data.

text.p: The dollar rose against the German mark and the Japanese yen on Thursday amid fresh signs of healthy U.S. economic growth with inflation under control.

The dollar, which had already recouped small losses overnight, took off in early New York trading on news that U.S. gross domestic product rose by 2.2 percent in the second quarter after climbing by a strong 4.9 percent pace in January through March.
In other good news, the report's inflation components drifted lower.
"Fundamentally the data was very good with very low inflation," said Tom Benfer, director of foreign exchange at Bank of Montreal.
The dollar got an added boost in late trading from U.S. Treasury Secretary Robert Rubin who reiterated his support of a strong dollar and its role in keeping inflation low.
"We have always said we believe a strong dollar is in our interest," Rubin told Reuters in an interview.
The dollar/yen rate edged up following Rubin's remarks that it was yet unclear whether domestic demand in Japan was robust enough to help the expansion.

Rubin also said the United States backs the International Monetary Fund's efforts to help Thailand cope with its worst economic crisis in a decade. As a result, the Thai currency, the baht, experienced some severe volatility lately.

But Rubin stressed the situation in Thailand was not similar to the financial crisis that rocked Mexico in 1994 and 1995, and would not require a U.S. aid package similar to the one the Clinton administration extended to Mexico then.
In late New York trade, the dollar was quoted at 1.8385 marks vs. 1.8370 marks late on Wednesday, and at 118.65 yen, up from 118.41 yen.
Traders reported some concern over the apparent disagreement between U.S. and Japanese carmakers regarding the appropriate level of the dollar/yen exchange rate.
A senior official at the Japanese Automobile Manufacturer's Association said a dollar above 120 yen would cause concern in his industry.
"Everytime we get close to 120 that's going to resurrect the trade issue," acknowledged Bank of Montreal's Benfer.

Meanwhile, American Automobile Manufacturer Association (AAMA) President Andrew Card presented a very different view, saying the yen was too weak against the dollar and should trade in the 95-to-105 range.
Incidents of official jawboning have increased in recent days, along with the dollar's latest push to a 2-1/2-month high of 118.95 yen on Wednesday.
Traders said market players remained cautious as they braced for the release on Friday of the July employment report.

Jobs data have been the focus of Wall Street lately due to fears that tight labour markets would drive wages higher and fuel higher inflation. This, in turn, may prompt the Federal Reserve to raise interest rates.
"People are not going to get too interested in trading right before the (employment) figures," said Kevin Lawrie, global foreign exchange manager at Mellon Bank.

"It's just exhaustion, but the dollar is poised very nicely going into tomorrow," added Lawrie, who did not expect the kind of "surprises that would get Federal Reserve Chairman Alan Greenspan to change his outlook on rates."
A rebound in the British pound vs. the mark contributed some to the dollar's rise, traders said.

Sterling also gained against the dollar, rising to $1.6403 from $1.6290 on Wednesday. The dollar was lower vs. the Swiss franc at 1.5120 compared with Wednesday's last quote at 1.5130 and lower at Canadian $1.3785 compared with C$1.3814.
